read.sections.0.heading.source: Small actions can help a community
read.sections.0.heading.back: Small actions can help a community

read.sections.0.text.note: 'Convention on the Rights of the Child' is 'Công ước về Quyền trẻ em' (the usual Vietnamese title). 'contribute' = 'đóng góp' (KEY_TERMS). Check that the rights sentences keep the meaning: the right to give views and the freedom to start or join groups and to meet.
read.sections.0.text.source: To contribute means to give your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to mean a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read with a younger child, translate for someone who is new, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that children have the right to give their views on things that affect them. It also says children are free to start or join groups and to meet together.
read.sections.0.text.back: To contribute means to give your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to be a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read a book with a little child, translate to help a newcomer, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help everyone learn, feel welcome and share the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that children have the right to state their opinion about things that affect them. The Convention also says children are free to form or join groups and meet each other.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Rights summarised in three short sentences. Check it does not weaken the idea.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: To contribute is to give your time or help to make things better. You do not need to do something big. Small acts help a community too. You can read with a young child. You can translate for a new learner. You can clean a room you share. You can join a club. The United Nations has a list of rights for children. It says children can give their views. It also says they can join groups.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: To contribute is to give your time or help to make things better. You do not need to do anything big. Small actions also help a community. You can read a book with a little child. You can translate to help a new learner. You can tidy a shared room. You can join a club. The United Nations has a list of children's rights. The list says children can state their opinion. The list also says children can join groups.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Start with evidence and work together
read.sections.1.heading.back: Start from evidence and work together

read.sections.1.text.note: 'stakeholder' = 'bên liên quan' (KEY_TERMS, flagged there as formal). 'upset people' as 'làm mọi người khó chịu'. 'Những người học' used for 'the learners' in the third person to stay consistent with 'learner' = 'người học'.
read.sections.1.text.source: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed litter near the bus stop outside. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, might upset people and would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include bus users, the learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns the evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager with one clear suggestion, such as a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.
read.sections.1.text.back: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed rubbish near the bus stop outside. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, may upset people and will not solve the problem. Idea 2 starts from evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask the people who use the bus stop what is missing. People affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include the bus riders, the learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager, with a clear suggestion, like a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: Check 'Bên liên quan là những người bị một vấn đề ảnh hưởng' is clear for a young reader.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Some learners saw litter near a bus stop. They had three ideas. Idea 1 was an angry post. It would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask bus users what is missing. Stakeholders are people who are affected by a problem. Bus users are stakeholders. So is the centre manager. Idea 3 is a short, polite letter to the manager. It asks for a new bin.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Some learners see rubbish near a bus stop. They have three ideas. Idea 1 is an angry post. It will not solve the problem. Idea 2 starts from evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask the bus riders what is missing. A stakeholder is someone affected by a problem. The bus riders are stakeholders. So is the centre manager. Idea 3 is a short, polite letter to the manager. The letter asks for a new bin.

read.sections.2.text.note: 'permission' is the glossary word 'cho phép' (verb form 'xin ... cho phép'), because Vietnamese has no neat noun. Check this is natural. 'liều lĩnh' for 'take risks'. | Review: English 'speak in public' (not 'before a crowd'); 'Who was included?' was a stiff passive. Native speaker to check 'được mời tham gia' for 'included'. [Reviewer changed: phát biểu trước đám đông → nói trước công chúng; Ai đã được tham gia? → Ai đã được mời tham gia?]
read.sections.2.text.source: Good contributions are safe. Before a clean-up, the learners talk to a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they take a photo of the litter, it should not show anyone's face or private information. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was included? What would we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.
read.sections.2.text.back: Good contributions are safe. Before a clean-up, the learners talk to a teacher and ask the centre manager for permission. They plan to use gloves and bags, and arrange for someone to take the rubbish away. If they photograph the pile of rubbish, the photo must not have the face of anyone or private information in it. You never need to speak before a crowd, post online or take risks in order to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who took part? Next time what will we do differently? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk to a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and bags. They plan where the rubbish goes. A photo must not show faces. You do not need to speak in public or post online. After you help, look back. What changed? Who was included? What can be better next time?
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk to a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and bags. They plan where to take the rubbish. Photos must not have faces. You do not need to speak before a crowd or post online. After helping, look back. What changed? Who took part? How can next time be better?
read.sections.2.simpler.note: Review: Same two fixes as the standard text. [Reviewer changed: phát biểu trước đám đông → nói trước công chúng; Ai đã được tham gia? → Ai đã được mời tham gia?]

write.example.source: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside our centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With our teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask our teacher and the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask users if they see a change.
write.example.back: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside the centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With our teacher, we will ask five bus riders. We will ask our teacher and the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask the users whether they notice a change.

watch.summary.note: 'young people' as 'người trẻ' (not 'thanh thiếu niên'). 'world leaders' as 'các nhà lãnh đạo thế giới'. Climate change: 'biến đổi khí hậu'. | Review: 'facts' rendered 'thông tin' (information); minor.
watch.summary.source: In this UNICEF video, young people share messages for world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places where they live. They ask leaders to listen to young people and to act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults and a real chance to change what happens. You do not have to speak to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading with a younger child or keeping a shared space clean.
watch.summary.back: In this UNICEF video, young people send a message to the world's leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places they live. They ask the leaders to listen to young people and act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about the problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to succeed, young people need information, help from adults and a real chance to change what happens. You do not need to talk to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading a book with a little child or keeping a shared space clean.
